To build an essay in five parts: introduction and thesis, arguments, counter-arguments, rebuttal, conclusion.
To introduce the thesis: a mio avviso, ritengo che / sono convinto che + subjunctive, la mia posizione è che.
To order your arguments: in primo luogo, inoltre, per di più, basti pensare a, a ciò si aggiunga che.
To concede and rebut: è pur vero che… tuttavia, si potrebbe obiettare che… ma, anche ammesso che + subjunctive.
To use impersonal formulas: è innegabile che, non si può negare che + subjunctive, va detto che.
To conclude: alla luce di quanto detto, in definitiva, per concludere.

The competition was called "Young Pens" and was organised every year by the Tuscany Region for secondary-school pupils. You entered with an argumentative essay of four pages at most, on the same prompt for everyone, announced on the first of June. The three winners would receive their prizes at the end of June in the Hall of the Five Hundred in Palazzo Vecchio, and their essays would be published in a regional daily. That year the prompt said: "Do art cities belong to those who live in them or to those who visit them? Discuss, with arguments and examples." Pietro's Italian teacher read it aloud in class, in the last week of school, and then looked at him. She said nothing. But the whole class turned to look at him, because everyone knew about the debate tournament, Researchers' Night, the trattoria in via Maggio. Pietro went red. That evening he signed up.

Bianca signed up too. Bianca had been his teammate in the debate tournament, the one who two years earlier had defended with him the thesis of tourism as a resource. She was the best in the class at Italian, spoke little and wrote beautifully, in short, precise sentences that seemed carved. The day after the prompt was announced, outside school, she told him she would argue the opposite thesis to his. "What thesis?" asked Pietro. "I haven't decided yet." Bianca smiled. "Yes you have," she said. "You'll say the city belongs to everyone, because your grandmother feeds whoever comes in. I'll say the city belongs to those who live in it. And we'll see who convinces the jury." Then she rode off on her bike, without waiting for an answer. Pietro stayed on the pavement watching her. Davide, who had heard everything, nudged him. "She's declared war on you," he said. "Or something else. I'm not sure."

That evening Pietro asked Bellini for advice; he was sitting at his table in the trattoria, with Doina's embroidered tablecloth and his newspaper open. He explained the prompt and said he didn't know where to begin. Bellini folded the newspaper calmly. "Do what a restorer does in front of a sick painting," he said. "Before touching anything, walk around it. Look at it from every side. Close up, from a distance, in raking light. Write down on a sheet everything you see, even the things you don't like. Especially those." Pietro asked what a painting had to do with an essay. Bellini smiled. "Everything," he said. "An essay is a restoration of ideas. You remove what is dirty, consolidate what is about to fall, and let what was underneath be seen. But if you start cleaning without having looked, you ruin everything." Pietro spent the evening filling a sheet with two columns: on the left the residents' reasons, on the right the visitors'. The right-hand column was shorter. That worried him.

Pietro wrote the first version in two evenings, in his room, with the window open onto the courtyard and the noises of the trattoria rising from the kitchen. It was three and a half pages long and began like this: "Florence is one of the most visited cities in the world. Every year millions of tourists arrive. Some think this is a good thing, others a bad thing." Then it explained the position of one side, then the other, with examples, figures, quotations. Only in the last paragraph, at the end of the third page, did it say what he thought. He was pleased. It seemed a balanced, complete, fair essay to him. The next morning he took it to the kitchen, where Graziella, back from hospital for a week, sat on the stool watching Karl with the same attention with which a general watches his troops. The doctor had forbidden her to stand for more than half an hour. She had interpreted the rule her own way.

Graziella read the essay with her glasses on the tip of her nose, while Karl chopped onions and pretended not to listen. It took her ten minutes. Then she put the sheets on the counter and said: "You've written three pages and I still don't understand what you think." Pietro explained that he said it at the end, that he first wanted to present both positions, impartially. Graziella shook her head. "Wrong," she said. "It's like a menu. If you write 'we have meat, fish, vegetables, bread, oil', the customer doesn't know what to order. First you name the dish: ribollita. Then the ingredients." She took a pencil and wrote at the top of the first page, in her crooked handwriting: "In my view…" "Start from here," she said. "Whoever reads it must know straight away which side you're on. Then you can explain everything you like. But first, your thesis."

Karl, who had listened to everything while chopping onions, looked up. "Graziella's right," he said. "Ruggeri says the same about degree theses. In my first week, in Rome, I took him a twenty-page chapter on the Madonna of Siena. He read it in five minutes, then asked me: 'What do you want to prove?' I didn't know. I'd collected data, photographs, analyses, but I had no thesis. He gave me the chapter back and said: 'Come back when you can answer in one sentence.'" Pietro asked how long it had taken him. "Three weeks," replied Karl. "For a single sentence. But then I wrote the rest in ten days." Graziella nodded, satisfied, as if that confirmation from Rome were her due. "You see?" she said to Pietro. "The professor and the cook say the same thing. When two such different people agree, they're usually right."

Pietro protested that his Italian teacher told them to be impartial. Graziella laughed. "The judge is impartial," she said. "You're the lawyer. You have to defend someone." Then, to Pietro's and Karl's great surprise, she explained the structure of an argumentative essay in five minutes, as if she had studied it for years. First the thesis. Then the arguments, in order, from strongest to weakest or weakest to strongest, "but always in order, like the courses of a lunch". Then what others say: "It could be objected that…" Then the answer: "It is true that… however…" You concede a little to your opponent, and then you take them apart. And at the end a single sentence, the one you want them to remember, "like dessert after lunch". Pietro looked at her open-mouthed. "Grandma," he said, "where did you learn to write an essay?" Graziella shrugged. "At the market," she said. "With the fishmonger. Forty years of haggling are better than secondary school."

Pietro threw away the first version and started again from scratch. This time he began with the thesis. It took him a whole day to find the right sentence, because he didn't want to say just "the city belongs to everyone", which seemed a postcard sentence to him. In the end he found it, one evening, watching his grandmother feed a Japanese tourist who didn't know a word of Italian. He wrote it at the top of the sheet: "In my view, an art city belongs neither only to those who live in it nor only to those who visit it, but to those who live in it and know how to welcome, and to those who visit it and know how to respect it." It was long, but it was his. He read it to Karl, who was cleaning the stove. Karl thought about it. "It's a hard thesis to defend," he said. "Because it's neither black nor white." "I know," replied Pietro. "But it's the true one." Karl nodded. "Then defend it well," he said. "True theses are the easiest to attack."

The arguments came more easily. Firstly, Pietro wrote, a city that doesn't welcome dies: one need only think of Venice, where the inhabitants leave and only tourists remain, but also of so many villages in the Apennines, where nobody goes any more and the houses fall down. A city needs people who arrive, just as a trattoria needs customers. Furthermore, visitors don't only bring money: they bring new eyes. He told the story of Karl, who came from Malta as an intern and became the cooperative's best letter writer; the story of Ion, a frightened Romanian railwayman who in 1990 ate his first ribollita in via Maggio. Finally, those who live in a city are not its owners, but its guardians, like the parishioners of San Leonardo with their Madonna. "It is undeniable," he wrote, "that those who live in a place have the right to protect it. But protecting doesn't mean closing the door."

Davide read the second version sitting on the trattoria steps, pencil in hand, as when he corrected his drawings. When he finished, he said it was good but too long. The competition rules said four pages at most, and Pietro had written five and a half. "You have to cut," said Davide. "Like Mancini with the reviews. Every word has to earn its place." Pietro protested that every sentence was important. Davide took the pencil and began crossing out, without asking permission: an adjective here, a repeated example there, a whole paragraph about the history of the trattoria that had nothing to do with the thesis. "This is beautiful," he said, "but it's not needed. Put it in the diary." Pietro looked at the sheet full of crossed-out lines and felt almost physical pain. Then he reread it from the start, skipping the struck-through parts. It was shorter, faster, clearer. It was better. "I hate it when you're right," he told Davide. "I know," replied Davide. "It happens a lot."

The hardest part was the counter-arguments. Pietro knew they existed, and that they were strong. Rising rents, shops closing, families leaving the centre, Guido the shoemaker driven out of via Toscanella, the magnet shops with David in his underpants. He knew them all, because he had seen them with his own eyes. For two days he couldn't write anything: every time he tried to answer, the answer seemed weak. It was Valeria who unblocked him. She came by the trattoria one afternoon, read the draft and told him something simple. "You mustn't deny the problems," she said. "You have to explain whose fault they are. It isn't the tourists' fault if rents go up. It's the fault of the rules that allow it." Pietro wrote: "It could be objected that mass tourism is emptying historic centres. It is true that rents have risen and many shops have closed; however, the fault lies not with those who visit, but with those who have failed to manage the visiting."

The next day, at the Biblioteca delle Oblate, Pietro met Bianca by chance. She was sitting at the table by the window, the one with a view of the dome, with a notebook and a pile of books. He had his laptop under his arm. They looked at each other, embarrassed. There were other free tables, but Pietro, without knowing why, sat down opposite her. They worked in silence for two hours, without looking at each other's pages. Every now and then Pietro looked up and saw her cross out a sentence, shake her head, rewrite it. Once she looked up at the same moment and he immediately lowered his eyes. At six, when the library closed, Bianca gathered her books and, before leaving, asked him a single question: "In your opinion, who defends a city when the tourists go home?" Pietro couldn't answer. Bianca smiled. "There," she said. "That's my thesis." And she left, leaving him with the question and with the dome turning orange in the sunset light.

For the conclusion, Pietro went back to the kitchen. Graziella was taking the afternoon rest the doctor had imposed on her, that is, she was sitting on the stool instead of standing. Pietro asked her what, in her opinion, the sentence to remember should be. Graziella thought for a long time, stirring the ribollita with the ladle. Then she said: "Write rule number one. My father's." Pietro understood. He wrote: "In the light of what has been said, I believe that an art city belongs to those who guard its memory and to those who are welcomed to get to know it. Ultimately, I think every city should have on its door the same rule my family's trattoria has had since 1950: whoever comes in, feed them. But remind them where they are." He reread the sentence. He had added the last part himself, without thinking. It seemed the truest thing he had ever written. He sent the essay that very evening, at five to midnight, five minutes before the deadline.

The three weeks of waiting passed slowly. Pietro helped at the trattoria, studied for his end-of-year exams, and every morning checked the post with his heart in his mouth. Graziella, meanwhile, was recovering. Dr Neri, at the check-up, said the new bypass was working beautifully and that she could go back to cooking, "but sitting down, and no more than four hours a day". Graziella listened respectfully and the next day cooked for six hours, standing up, because, she said, the doctor had said four hours sitting, but hadn't mentioned hours standing. Karl, who had by now become her right hand, watched her anxiously and brought her the stool every half hour. She refused it every half hour. It was a little ritual repeated all day long, like a ballet, which the regulars began to follow with interest, betting on who would give in first. At the end of the week, Graziella sat down. Once. Karl recorded it in his notebook as a victory.

Three weeks later a letter arrived from the Region. Pietro opened it in the kitchen, in front of Graziella and Karl, with trembling hands. He was among the ten finalists. On the twenty-eighth of June, in the Hall of the Five Hundred, the three winners would be announced, in the presence of the President of the Region and a jury of writers and journalists. The next day, coming out of the municipal swimming pool, Pietro met Bianca. She was among the finalists too. They looked at each other for a moment without saying anything. Then Bianca smiled. "I've read your thesis," she said. "The Region's press release publishes the first lines of every finalist essay." Pietro asked what she thought of it. Bianca thought about it, a towel over her shoulders and her hair wet. "It's beautiful," she said. "But it has a flaw. It's too kind. The jury wants someone who fights." Then she added, before leaving: "I fought. You'll see."

That evening Pietro reread his essay ten times, looking for the flaw Bianca had talked about. He found it on the fifth reading. It was true: it was too kind. It presented the counter-arguments with so much care, so much understanding, that in the end it almost seemed to agree with them. He ran to Mancini, at the newspaper office, and asked whether anything could still be changed. Mancini looked at him over his glasses, with the cat Titolo asleep on his knees. "A submitted essay is like a printed article," he said. "You don't touch it any more. You can only learn for next time." Pietro sat down, disheartened. Mancini stroked the cat. "And besides," he added, "who says kindness is a flaw? I've read thousands of articles that shouted. I remember very few of them. The ones I remember are the ones that made me think. Sometimes a kind essay loses the competition and wins the memory." Pietro didn't entirely understand. He understood three weeks later.

On the evening of the twenty-eighth of June the Hall of the Five Hundred was lit up as if for a party. Pietro had been there many times, on school trips, to look at the battle frescoes on the walls, but he had never seen it like this: the chairs lined up under the gilded ceiling, the photographers, the President of the Region in a jacket and tie, the ten finalists sitting in the front row with their parents behind. Graziella had come, despite the doctor. She had put on her coat for great occasions even though it was June and hot, and sat in the third row between Marco and Bellini, with Karl, Davide and Valeria beside them. Bianca was sitting two seats from Pietro, in a blue dress with her hair up. She never turned to look at him. But when the President went up on stage and everyone fell silent, Pietro noticed that her hands were clasped in her lap so tightly that her knuckles were white. She was afraid too.

The president of the jury was an elderly writer, author of novels Pietro had read at school, with short grey hair and a deep voice. Before announcing the winners, she said a few words about the essays. She said that this year the jury had read four hundred texts, and that many were good but few were essays: they were compositions, stories, outbursts. "An essay," she said, "is not an opinion. It is an opinion that has the courage to look its opponent in the face." Then she announced the third prize: a boy from Lucca, who had written about tourism in the Cinque Terre. Then the second: a girl from Arezzo, about her village emptying. Pietro felt his heart beating in his ears. Bianca, beside him, had closed her eyes. "The first prize," said the writer, "goes to an essay that struck us with the force with which it fights the thesis opposite to its own. The title is: 'The city is not a hotel'. The author is Bianca Sereni."

The hall applauded. Bianca opened her eyes, stood up, turned for a second towards Pietro, with an expression he couldn't decipher, and went up on stage to collect her prize. Pietro applauded with everyone else. He felt something strange in his stomach, half disappointment and half pride, as when he had lost his first game of chess against Bellini. Then the writer took the microphone again. "This year the jury has also decided to award an honourable mention," she said. "It isn't a prize. It's recognition for an essay that didn't win because it is too kind to its opponents, but which contains the most beautiful sentence we have read this year." Pietro heard Davide, behind him, hold his breath. "The sentence is this: 'Whoever comes in, feed them. But remind them where they are.' The author is Pietro." In the third row, Graziella stood up and applauded on her own, before everyone else, in her coat for great occasions.

At the end of the ceremony, while the photographers surrounded Bianca, the elderly writer came up to Pietro. She shook his hand and told him she had read his essay three times. "It's the essay of someone who is afraid of hurting his opponents," she said. "That's a fine quality in a person. In an essay, slightly less so." Pietro blushed. The writer smiled. "Don't stop being kind," she went on. "But learn to arm your kindness. You can concede that someone is right and then show firmly that they're wrong. It's not cruelty: it's respect. You treat your opponent as an intelligent person, able to bear a good argument." Then she asked him where that sentence about the door came from. Pietro told her about the trattoria, great-grandfather Renzo, 1950, the man in the coat full of holes. The writer listened to the end, then took out a notebook and wrote something down. "That story," she said, "someone will steal from me one day. Better if you write it first."

After the ceremony, in the courtyard of Palazzo Vecchio, under the decorated columns, Bianca came up to Pietro with her prize in her hand, a small silver plaque with the lily of Florence. For a moment neither of them knew what to say. Then Bianca handed him her essay, printed, and asked him to read it. Pietro read it there, standing, under the fountain with the cherub. It was beautifully written, in short, sharp sentences. The thesis was clear from the first line: "The city belongs to those who live in it, because only those who live in it defend it after the tourists have gone." And the counter-arguments were exactly his: the trattorias that welcome, the visitors who bring new eyes, the restorations paid for by tickets. Bianca presented them all, honestly, and then took them apart one by one. The most beautiful paragraph said: "It could be objected that a closed city dies. True; however, a city turned into a hotel dies twice: first it loses its inhabitants, then it loses its soul."

Pietro handed the essay back. "You won," he said. "And you're right about one thing. I didn't fight enough." Bianca shook her head. "You wrote the sentence everyone remembers," she replied. "I wrote the essay that wins. They're two different things." Then she did something Pietro didn't expect: she took a pen out of her bag and, under her thesis, on the last page, wrote a line by hand. She showed it to him. It said: "Even granting that I'm right, your sentence is more beautiful than mine." Pietro laughed. Davide, watching them from a distance with Karl, said quietly that that was a declaration of something, but that he was no longer sure it was a declaration of war. Karl nudged him. Graziella, who had seen everything from the bench where she had sat down to rest, turned to Bellini. "I like that girl," she said. "She knows how to argue. And she knows how to lose when she wins."

The following Sunday, the regional daily published Bianca's essay over a whole page, with her photograph. Underneath, in a small box, was the honourable-mention sentence, with Pietro's name. Mancini, at the "Gazzetta dell'Oltrarno", went further: he published the two essays side by side, in two columns, with a headline that made the whole neighbourhood laugh: "Whose city? Two kids, two theses, one ribollita." And underneath, in italics, he added an editorial note: "Readers are invited to write in saying which of the two essays convinced them more. Please note that Signora Graziella has already voted, and that her vote counts double." A hundred and twenty letters arrived. Sixty-one for Bianca, fifty-nine for Pietro. Mancini published the result with a one-line comment: "The stronger thesis won. But the kinder thesis lost by only two votes. Perhaps the city is kinder than we think."

That evening Pietro opened the black notebook and stuck in the letter from the Region, the page from the "Gazzetta" and, next to it, the line Bianca had handwritten under her thesis, which she had given him by tearing out the last page of her essay. Then he wrote, as always, what he had learned. "One: the thesis comes at the beginning, like the dish on the menu. Two: an essay without opponents is an advert. Three: you can be right and lose, and be wrong and win; what matters is knowing why." He reread the list. Then, below, he added a line that had nothing to do with essays. "Four: Bianca writes better than me. I have to learn to fight. I asked her to teach me. She said yes, but that in exchange I have to teach her ribollita. I told her I can get to ninety-eight per cent. She laughed." He closed the notebook, turned off the light and lay awake for a long time, looking at the ceiling, smiling without really knowing why.

The following week Bianca came to the trattoria for her first ribollita lesson, as they had agreed. She arrived at six in the afternoon, with a new notebook and a pencil, and Graziella looked her up and down with the same look she gave new suppliers. Then she asked her, without preamble: "In your view, does garlic go in ribollita?" Bianca thought for a moment. "In my view, no," she replied. "But it could be objected that many recipes include it. That's true; however, written recipes aren't the real recipes." Karl, at the stove, nearly dropped the ladle. Graziella was silent for a long moment. Then she turned to Pietro. "Marry this one," she said. Pietro went as red as the sauce. Bianca laughed so hard she had to lean on the counter. Davide, who had dropped in by chance, said that sentence absolutely had to go in the diary, and that if Pietro didn't write it, he would draw it.

The thesis and conclusion of Pietro's essay. Read and answer.

It is true that rents have risen; however, the fault lies not with those who visit, but with those who have failed to manage the visiting.
Ultimately: whoever comes in, feed them. But remind them where they are.

Write an argumentative essay (at least 280 words) on one of these topics: "Should mobile phones be banned at school?", "Is it better to live in the city or in the countryside?", "Is tourism a resource or a threat for your town?". Follow the five-part structure.
I stated the thesis in the first paragraph (a mio avviso, ritengo che + subjunctive).
I gave at least three arguments in order (in primo luogo, inoltre, infine) with an example (basti pensare a).
I presented a counter-argument (si potrebbe obiettare che, alcuni sostengono che).
I rebutted it (è pur vero che… tuttavia, anche ammesso che + subjunctive).
I concluded without new arguments (alla luce di quanto detto, in definitiva).
In recent years there has been much discussion about using phones at school. In my view, they should be banned during lessons, but not during break.
Firstly, the phone is distracting: one need only think how many times we look at it in an hour. Furthermore, it reduces conversation between classmates.
It could be objected that the phone is useful for studying. That's true; however, schools already have computers.
In the light of what has been said, I believe the solution isn't banning, but teaching how to use it.
